assessmentSummary.identity: Supine dead bug with a medicine ball held by a declared contralateral hand-and-knee press while the free opposite arm and leg move and return under rib-pelvis control.
currentCardFindings: The legacy name and generic description omit ball position and limb contract.
The exact family reference defines a contralateral hand-knee press and opposite arm-leg motion.
The ball must not be treated as a generic weight, toss, or interchangeable wall.
Five candidates have healthy oEmbed metadata only; no human media approval is created.

currentCardSnapshot.description: Perform Medicine Ball Dead Bug Press with a medicine ball to train low-threat anterior core activation and rib-pelvis control before harder work. The load, distance, partner input, and volume should preserve the card's phase intent.

claims: The medicine-ball version presses the ball between one hand and the opposite knee while the free opposite arm and leg extend.
Its stable identity is a contralateral movable-ball press with declared free-limb motion; it remains distinct from both hands pressing a fixed wall.
Taxonomy must declare supine anti-extension, the moving limbs, the pressing limbs, return position, cadence, and breath.
The card must not use a proficiency classification; variant difficulty is exercise complexity and physical difficulty.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic activity of selected trunk muscles during dynamic spine stabilization exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
claims: Dying-bug progressions recruit the abdominal wall while limb motion challenges lumbopelvic control.
Declare abdominal-wall, hip-flexor, latissimus and shoulder-stabilizer roles plus spine, pelvis, hip and shoulder joints without claiming isolated activation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Changes in muscle activity of the abdominal muscles according to exercise method and speed during dead bug exercise
claims: Limb selection and movement speed alter abdominal muscle activity during dead-bug exercise.
Observable gates are rib-pelvis control, lumbar position, declared press continuity, smooth limb travel, symmetric return, and breathing.

evidence.sourceTitle: Changes in muscle activity of the abdominal muscles according to exercise method and speed during dead bug exercise
claims: Changing moving limbs, lever length, press constraint, range, and tempo changes task demand.
Score exact variants on exercise complexity and physical difficulty, and derive overall difficulty as their maximum.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic activity of selected trunk muscles during dynamic spine stabilization exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
claims: Dead-bug recruitment remains submaximal in the cited healthy sample and rises with harder progressions.
Track abdominal and hip-flexor fatigue, breath compensation, rib flare, lumbar motion, press loss, neck tension, and recovery before higher-cost trunk work.
External press variations require a stable floor plus an exact wall or ball setup.
Declare surface, head and hand clearance, wall integrity or ball size and mass, lighting, observation angle, shared-station traffic, and sanitation.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic activity of selected trunk muscles during dynamic spine stabilization exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
claims: Progression changes recruitment, so dosage should stop before a harder pattern replaces the declared one.
Use low-to-moderate controlled repetitions per side, a full return, and enough rest to preserve press, posture, range, and breath.
Instruction should establish the supine start, stacked ribs and pelvis, controlled limb motion, and return.
Name exactly what presses, what moves, the range, exhale, return, side change, and stop signal.
Dead-bug variations should be regressed when the athlete cannot maintain the intended trunk position.
Stop for pain, pressure or neurologic symptoms, dizziness, breath panic, neck strain, lumbar lift or arch, rib flare, press loss, uncontrolled limb drop, or material asymmetry.

evidence.sourceTitle: Electromyographic activity of selected trunk muscles during dynamic spine stabilization exercises
evidence.sourcePublisher: Archives of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation
claims: Dead-bug progressions are controlled trunk-stabilization exercises rather than ballistic or conditioning tasks.
Use early for low-fatigue trunk organization or later for controlled trunk capacity; do not race repetitions.
Athlete support should show the start shape, pressing surfaces, moving limbs, end range, breath, return, and self-check.
Offer shorter levers, smaller range, one moving limb, less press, fewer repetitions, longer rest, and text or image instruction.

evidence.sourceTitle: Changes in muscle activity of the abdominal muscles according to exercise method and speed during dead bug exercise
claims: Coach support should expose exact limb pattern, press target, range, tempo, side, dose, observation angle, compensation, symptoms, and shutdown.
Record whether posture, press, breath, limb path, and return remained repeatable.
The dead bug admits multiple limb and external-constraint regressions.
Accessibility options include one limb at a time, heel taps, shorter reach, tactile target, lighter or larger ball, fewer repetitions, longer rest, and nonvideo instructions.
Wall press and contralateral medicine-ball press are different constraint contracts within the dead-bug family.
Unloaded heel taps, stability-ball dead bugs, overhead-loaded dead bugs, band pulldowns, hollow holds, and bird dogs require explicit variant or definition review.
YouTube supports privacy-enhanced embedding through youtube-nocookie.com.
The supplied links have healthy current oEmbed metadata only; full viewing, exact contract, cue quality, safety, captions, accessibility, reviewer identity, and approval remain unresolved.

alternateAssessments.name: Single Free-Limb Control
alternateAssessments.rationale: Only one free limb moves while the contralateral ball press remains fixed.

alternateAssessments.name: Contralateral Arm-Leg Extension
alternateAssessments.rationale: The free opposite arm and leg extend together while the ball stays pressed.

alternateAssessments.name: Stability-Ball Dead Bug Press
alternateAssessments.rationale: A larger compressible ball can preserve the press and limb sequence when size is recorded.

alternateAssessments.name: Dead Bug Wall Press
alternateAssessments.rationale: Both hands press a fixed wall while the arms do not move.

alternateAssessments.name: Medicine-Ball Dead Bug Toss
alternateAssessments.rationale: Releasing and catching the ball changes the task to reactive object control.

alternateAssessments.name: Loaded Overhead Dead Bug
alternateAssessments.rationale: Holding an external load overhead changes force direction and limb availability.
